steps.title: Distance is a small effect
steps.say: Good catch — but distance barely matters. Earth's orbit is almost circular, so the Earth–Sun distance changes by only about 3%, which alters sunlight by roughly 7%. That is far too small to explain summer and winter.

ops.text:
Distance changes by only ~3%.
Sunlight intensity changes ~7% — too small.

Tilt matters far more. It changes:
1) how steeply sunlight hits the ground
2) how many hours of daylight

steps.title: Which position is which season
steps.say: Since the axis always leans the same way, the north pole tilts toward the Sun on the left side of the orbit and away from it on the right — so those are northern summer and northern winter.

ops.text:
Northern summer
N pole toward Sun

Northern winter
N pole
away from Sun

steps.title: Why that makes it hotter
steps.say: So northern summer is hotter not because we are closer, but because sunlight arrives more directly and the days are longer.

ops.text:
Steeper sunlight = more energy per area.
Longer days = more hours of heating.
Together: warmer summer.
